ieltsReading.title: Learning in the garden
ieltsReading.text: When the primary school in a small town near the river opened its garden five years ago, many parents were doubtful. The head teacher, Ms Sophea, wanted children to learn science and maths by growing vegetables, but some families worried that it would take time away from reading and writing. Today, the garden covers about half of the school's land. Each class looks after its own section, and pupils measure how fast the plants grow, record the weather and calculate how much they can sell at the weekly market. The money pays for books and for school trips. According to the school's own records, pupils' maths results have improved every year since the garden began, although Ms Sophea admits that a new maths teacher, who joined at the same time, may also have made a difference. Not every school could copy the idea: the garden needs water all year, and in the dry season older pupils carry it from a well. Several schools in the province have visited, and two have started small gardens of their own.

statements.text: Some parents were not sure about the garden at first.
statements.why: "Many parents were doubtful."

statements.text: The garden is bigger than the school buildings.
statements.why: It covers half of the land; the buildings' size is never given.

statements.text: Every class grows the same vegetables.
statements.why: Each class has its own section, but the text does not say what they grow.

statements.text: Money from the market is spent on books.
statements.why: "The money pays for books and for school trips."

statements.text: Ms Sophea thinks the garden is the only reason maths results improved.
statements.why: She admits the new maths teacher may also have made a difference.

statements.text: In the dry season the garden's water comes from the river.
statements.why: Older pupils carry it from a well.

ieltsReading.title: Why we forget new words
ieltsReading.text: In the 1880s, the German researcher Hermann Ebbinghaus tested his own memory by learning lists of nonsense syllables and checking how many he could remember after different amounts of time. He found that most forgetting happens soon after learning: a lot is lost within the first day, and after that it is lost more slowly. He also found that reviewing material several times, with gaps between the reviews, made it last much longer than studying it many times in one sitting. Modern researchers call this the spacing effect, and many studies since then have confirmed it. Some language-learning apps now use it to decide when to show each word again. However, scientists point out that memory also depends on other things, such as sleep, interest in the subject and whether a word is used in real conversation. A word that you say to a friend may be remembered better than one you only read on a screen.

statements.text: Ebbinghaus tested his ideas on other people.
statements.why: He tested his own memory.

statements.text: Forgetting is fastest soon after learning.
statements.why: "Most forgetting happens soon after learning."

statements.text: Other scientists of his time did not accept Ebbinghaus's work.
statements.why: The text says nothing about how scientists of his time reacted.

statements.text: Studying something many times in one session works better than spaced reviews.
statements.why: Spaced reviews made it last much longer.

statements.text: Sleep can affect how well we remember.
statements.why: Memory "also depends on other things, such as sleep".

statements.text: Most language-learning apps use the spacing effect.
statements.why: It says "some" apps use it; it does not say how many.

ieltsReading.title: The night market
ieltsReading.text: Every Friday and Saturday evening, the car park behind the town's main bus station becomes a night market. It started three years ago with about twenty food stalls, and it now has more than eighty, selling clothes, phone accessories and handmade jewellery as well as food. The market is run by a group of local sellers rather than by the town council, and each stall pays a small fee to cover cleaning and electricity. Most visitors are young people who come after work or college, but on Saturdays many families bring their children for the live music. The organisers say that the market has helped people who lost their jobs to start small businesses. Not everyone is happy, however. Some shop owners in the town centre complain that they have lost customers since the market opened, and people living nearby have asked for the music to end earlier. The organisers have agreed to stop the music at ten o'clock, but they say they have no plans to open on weekdays.

statements.text: The market takes place in a car park.
statements.why: "The car park behind the town's main bus station becomes a night market."

statements.text: The town council runs the market.
statements.why: It is run by local sellers "rather than by the town council".

statements.text: The stall fee has gone up since the market opened.
statements.why: The fee is mentioned, but not whether it has changed.

statements.text: Families mostly come on Saturdays.
statements.why: "On Saturdays many families bring their children."

statements.text: Some shop owners are unhappy about the market.
statements.why: They "complain that they have lost customers".

statements.text: The market will soon open on weekdays too.
statements.why: They "have no plans to open on weekdays".

ieltsReading.title: Bicycles made of bamboo
ieltsReading.text: In a small workshop outside a city, a group of young people builds bicycle frames from bamboo. The project began four years ago, when an engineering student noticed how much bamboo grew around her village and wondered whether it could replace steel. Bamboo is light and strong, and it absorbs the shock of bumpy roads, which makes riding more comfortable. Each frame takes about two weeks to make by hand, and the team now sells around thirty bicycles a month, mostly to customers abroad. The bicycles cost more than ordinary ones, but buyers say they last well if they are kept dry. The founder hopes to open a training centre so that other villages can start similar workshops. However, she admits that finding reliable glue, which has to be imported, has been a constant problem.

statements.text: The project was started by an engineering student.
statements.why: "An engineering student noticed how much bamboo grew around her village."

statements.text: Bamboo makes riding on bumpy roads less comfortable.
statements.why: It absorbs the shock, "which makes riding more comfortable".

statements.text: Most of the bicycles are sold to customers in other countries.
statements.why: They are sold "mostly to customers abroad".

statements.text: The team makes about thirty frames a week.
statements.why: About thirty bicycles a month; each frame takes about two weeks.

statements.text: The bamboo bicycles are cheaper than ordinary ones.
statements.why: "The bicycles cost more than ordinary ones."

statements.text: The glue the team uses comes from Japan.
statements.why: The glue is imported, but the text does not say from where.

ieltsReading.title: Sleep and learning
ieltsReading.text: Many students stay up late before exams, but research suggests that this may be a mistake. During sleep, the brain appears to replay and strengthen what was learned during the day. In one well-known type of experiment, people learn a list of words or a simple task, and then either sleep or stay awake for several hours before they are tested. Those who sleep usually remember more. Short naps can also help, although they seem to be most useful when they last less than an hour. Scientists are less certain about how much sleep different people need: most adults need between seven and nine hours, but the right amount varies. Caffeine late in the day can reduce the quality of sleep, even for people who say they sleep well after coffee.

statements.text: Staying up late before an exam is always a good idea.
statements.why: Research suggests "this may be a mistake".

statements.text: In these experiments, people who slept usually remembered more.
statements.why: "Those who sleep usually remember more."

statements.text: Naps longer than two hours help memory most.
statements.why: Naps seem most useful when they last less than an hour.

statements.text: Scientists know exactly how much sleep each person needs.
statements.why: Scientists are "less certain"; the right amount varies.

statements.text: Most adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep.
statements.why: "Most adults need between seven and nine hours."

statements.text: Coffee affects children's sleep more than adults' sleep.
statements.why: Children are not mentioned.

ieltsReading.title: Schools on the water
ieltsReading.text: In some parts of the world, floods make it impossible for children to reach school for weeks every year. One solution has been the floating school: a boat that collects children from riverside villages and holds lessons on board. The idea was first tried by a local charity in a river delta, and it has since been copied in several other countries. A typical floating school has one classroom, a small library and solar panels that power lights and a few laptops. Teachers say that attendance has improved, especially among girls, whose families had worried about long journeys on foot. However, the boats are expensive to maintain, and most depend on donations. Some governments have started to pay part of the costs.

statements.text: Floods can stop children from getting to school.
statements.why: Floods "make it impossible for children to reach school".

statements.text: A government built the first floating school.
statements.why: It was "first tried by a local charity".

statements.text: Floating schools use solar power.
statements.why: They have "solar panels that power lights and a few laptops".

statements.text: Each floating school has several classrooms.
statements.why: A typical one "has one classroom".

statements.text: Fewer boys go to school since the floating schools began.
statements.why: The text says girls' attendance improved; it says nothing about boys falling.

statements.text: All floating schools are now paid for by governments.
statements.why: Most depend on donations; some governments pay part.

ieltsReading.title: Planting a coastline
ieltsReading.text: Ten years ago, the beach in front of one small fishing village was losing about a metre of land every year. Storms pulled the sand away, and several families had to move their houses further inland. A local teacher suggested planting mangroves, trees that grow in salty water and hold the mud together with their roots. At first, many villagers were doubtful. Some worried that the trees would block their view of the sea. To make matters worse, the first two hundred young trees were washed away by a storm only a month after they were planted. The teacher did not give up. With help from a university team, the villagers learned to plant when the sea is calmer and to protect each young tree with a low bamboo fence. Today, a strip of mangroves about four hundred metres long stands between the village and the sea. The land has stopped disappearing, and fishermen say they now catch more crabs near the trees, because young sea animals hide among the roots. Visitors have also started to come, and some families now earn extra money by taking them on small boats through the forest. Every year, schoolchildren help to plant new trees, and each class looks after its own section. However, not everyone is happy. A few fishermen complain that the trees make it harder to reach their old fishing spots, and the village has not yet agreed on how many new trees to plant next year.

statements.text: The idea of planting mangroves came from a teacher.
statements.why: "A local teacher suggested planting mangroves."

statements.text: All of the first young trees survived.
statements.why: The first two hundred trees "were washed away by a storm only a month after they were planted".

statements.text: The villagers learned to plant when the sea is calmer.
statements.why: They "learned to plant when the sea is calmer".

statements.text: The university paid for the young trees.
statements.why: A university team helped, but the text does not say who paid for the trees.

statements.text: Fishermen catch fewer crabs since the mangroves grew.
statements.why: Fishermen "now catch more crabs near the trees".

statements.text: Everyone in the village is happy with the mangroves.
statements.why: "Not everyone is happy." A few fishermen complain about reaching their fishing spots.

ieltsReading.title: A library on wheels
ieltsReading.text: Every Tuesday morning, an old yellow bus stops outside a primary school in a village forty kilometres from the nearest town. Inside, the seats have been replaced with shelves holding about two thousand books. The bus belongs to a small charity that started with one driver and one librarian. Before the bus came, the school had only a single cupboard of books, most of them old textbooks. Now each child can borrow two books a week, and the librarian reads a story aloud to the youngest classes while older pupils help younger ones to choose their books. Teachers say that children who borrow regularly have become more confident readers, although the charity admits it has not measured this properly. The books come from donations, and most of them are in Khmer, with a smaller number in English. Running the bus is not cheap. Fuel is the largest cost, and in the rainy season some roads become so muddy that the bus cannot reach three of the villages on its route. When this happens, the librarian carries a box of books on a motorbike instead. Recently, a group of former students who grew up visiting the bus raised enough money to buy a second one. They hope it will start a new route in the north of the province next year.

statements.text: The bus has shelves where the seats used to be.
statements.why: "The seats have been replaced with shelves."

statements.text: Before the bus came, the school had a large library.
statements.why: It "had only a single cupboard of books".

statements.text: Each child can borrow three books a week.
statements.why: "Each child can borrow two books a week."

statements.text: The charity has carefully measured how children's reading has improved.
statements.why: The charity "admits it has not measured this properly".

statements.text: Fuel is the charity's biggest cost for the bus.
statements.why: "Fuel is the largest cost."

statements.text: The librarian's motorbike was a gift from a teacher.
statements.why: The librarian uses a motorbike, but the text does not say where it came from.

statements.text: The government paid for a second bus.
statements.why: Former students "raised enough money to buy a second one".

ieltsReading.title: Calling a ride
ieltsReading.text: In many Asian cities, the way people take short trips has changed quickly. Not long ago, a passenger who wanted a ride usually stood at the side of the road and agreed on a price with a driver before getting in. Today, many people open an app on their phone instead. The app shows the price before the trip starts, and the passenger can follow the route on a map. Payment can also be made through the app, so there is no need to carry cash. Some passengers say they feel safer, too, because the app records the driver's name and the route of every trip. For visitors who do not speak the local language, this removes one of the most stressful parts of travelling. Drivers have mixed feelings. Some say the apps bring them more customers, especially at night. Others complain that the companies take a share of every fare, so a long day of work earns them less than it used to. Older drivers often find the apps difficult to use and still prefer to wait outside markets and hotels. City planners are interested in the information the apps collect, because it shows which streets are busiest at different times of day. One city has already used this information to change the timing of its traffic lights. Whether apps will reduce traffic, however, is still not clear, because cheap rides may also encourage people to travel more often.

statements.text: Passengers used to agree on a price before the trip.
statements.why: A passenger "agreed on a price with a driver before getting in".

statements.text: The apps make travelling easier for visitors who do not speak the local language.
statements.why: The apps remove "one of the most stressful parts of travelling" for these visitors.

statements.text: All drivers are happy with the apps.
statements.why: "Drivers have mixed feelings", and some complain.

statements.text: The app companies take part of every fare.
statements.why: "The companies take a share of every fare."

statements.text: Older drivers find the apps easy to use.
statements.why: "Older drivers often find the apps difficult to use."

statements.text: The apps are more popular with women than with men.
statements.why: The text does not compare men and women.

statements.text: It is certain that the apps will reduce traffic.
statements.why: Whether apps will reduce traffic "is still not clear".

ieltsReading.title: Learning with short breaks
ieltsReading.text: A group of teachers at a language school decided to test a simple idea: would students remember new words better if they took short breaks during a lesson? Sixty adult students took part, and all the words were nouns connected with travel, such as luggage and departure. Half of them studied forty words for fifty minutes without stopping. The other half studied the same words, but stopped every twelve minutes for a two-minute break, during which they stood up, looked out of the window and did not talk. One week later, both groups took the same test without warning. The students who had taken breaks remembered about a fifth more words than the others. Another result surprised the teachers. When the students were asked how much they thought they had learned, the group without breaks felt more confident, even though they actually did worse. One teacher suggested that working without stopping feels productive, so students believe it must be effective. The teachers are careful not to claim too much. Their study was small, it took place in only one school, and all the students were adults. The breaks were also short and quiet, and the teachers do not know whether checking a phone during a break would have the same effect. Even so, the school has now added short breaks to all its evening classes, and several students say the lessons feel less tiring.

statements.text: Both groups studied the same words.
statements.why: The second half "studied the same words".

statements.text: The students knew they would be tested after a week.
statements.why: They took the test "without warning".

statements.text: The students who took breaks remembered more words.
statements.why: They "remembered about a fifth more words than the others".

statements.text: The students without breaks thought they had learned less.
statements.why: The group without breaks "felt more confident".

statements.text: The study took place in several schools.
statements.why: "It took place in only one school."

statements.text: The teachers plan to repeat the study with teenagers.
statements.why: The text mentions that all the students were adults, but says nothing about future studies.

statements.text: The school has added short breaks to all its evening classes.
statements.why: "The school has now added short breaks to all its evening classes."

lines.text: Would you like us to prepare a birthday cake? It's fifteen dollars.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Yes, please. A chocolate one.

ieltsListening.title: Renting a flat
ieltsListening.intro: A man phones about a flat to rent. Complete the form.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Hello, City Homes. How can I help?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I'm calling about the flat on Street sixty-three.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Ah yes, the two-bedroom flat. It's on the fourth floor.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Is there a lift?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, there is. The rent is three hundred and fifty dollars a month.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Does that include water?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Water, yes, but not electricity.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: When can I see it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: How about Thursday at ten in the morning?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Perfect. My family name is Kim. That's K, I, M.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Thank you, Mr Kim. Please bring your passport.

ieltsListening.title: Joining a gym
ieltsListening.intro: A woman joins a gym. Complete the form.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Welcome to FitLife. Are you interested in joining?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Yes. What kinds of membership do you have?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Monthly is forty dollars, or you can pay four hundred for a whole year.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I'll take the yearly one.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Great. Can I have your full name?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Sophea Long. Long is L, O, N, G.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: And your date of birth?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: The second of September, nineteen ninety-eight.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Do you have any health problems we should know about?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Only a bad back, from an old injury.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: OK, we'll tell your trainer. Your first session is on Monday at six thirty in the evening.

ieltsListening.title: Buying a bus ticket
ieltsListening.intro: A man phones a bus company to buy a ticket. Complete the form.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Good afternoon, River Line Buses. How can I help you?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Hi. I'd like a ticket from Phnom Penh to Siem Reap, please.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Sure. Which day are you travelling?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: On Friday, the twenty-second of March.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: We have buses at eight in the morning, eleven in the morning and two in the afternoon.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: The eleven o'clock one, please. Eight is too early for me.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: No problem. That's fifteen dollars. Can I have your family name?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Yes, it's Kong. K, O, N, G.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Thank you. Would you like a window seat or an aisle seat?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: A window seat, please.

ieltsListening.title: Joining a library
ieltsListening.intro: A student asks about joining a city library. Complete the form.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Hello, can I help you?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Yes, I'd like to join the library, please.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Of course. Can I have your first name?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: It's Sophea. S, O, P, H, E, A.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Thanks. And your date of birth?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: The ninth of July, two thousand and four. How many books can I borrow?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Up to six at a time, and you can keep them for three weeks.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Is there a cost for the card?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It's free for students. But if you lose it, a new card costs two dollars.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: OK. And what time do you close on Sundays?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: On Sundays we open at nine and close at one in the afternoon.

ieltsListening.title: Seeing a doctor
ieltsListening.intro: A woman phones a clinic to make an appointment. Complete the form.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Good morning, Riverside Clinic.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Hello. I'd like to see a doctor, please. I've had a sore throat for four days.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: I'm sorry to hear that. What's your family name?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: It's Chan. C, H, A, N.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The earliest appointment is tomorrow, Tuesday, at a quarter past ten.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Tuesday is difficult for me. Do you have anything on Wednesday?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, Wednesday at three forty-five in the afternoon.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That's perfect. How much will it cost?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It's twelve dollars for a first visit. We only take cash at the moment, I'm afraid.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That's fine. Thank you.

ieltsListening.title: A cooking course
ieltsListening.intro: A man asks about a weekend cooking course. Complete the form.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Hello, Spice Garden Cooking School.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Hi. I'm calling about your course for beginners.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. It runs on Saturday mornings for five weeks.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: When does the next one start?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: On the first of June. Classes begin at eight thirty.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And how much is it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Ninety dollars for the whole course, including all the ingredients. You just need to bring an apron.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Great. I'd like to sign up. My name's Visal. V, I, S, A, L.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Thanks, Visal. And your email address?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: It's visal dot chef at example dot com.
